title: The Pompous One: From Sublime to Ridiculous in Prelude and Fugue No.11, Book I
content_blocks: This Prelude and Fugue uses a transposition of the same mode as No.3 (E; see “The Alarmist,” coming September 6, 2025), in which black keys are heavily represented:  25 of the 45 tones across the piano are black keys.  This black/white balance sets up the start of the prelude, playing through the black keys in increasingly large scalar segments, generating a pentatonic sound.  Slowly the white keys start infiltrating the black; as the pentatonic sound changes, the scales get longer and start overlapping themselves, eventually creating a three-part texture that highlight’s the mode’s major and minor sixths.  As the texture then thins out, the rhythmic density increases, featuring a direct contrast and tension between the white and the black keys of the mode.  The increasingly-energetic lines reach to the top of the piano, leading to falling white-key arpeggios that bring us to the bottom of the piano, which then similarly rises back to the top.  Following a white-key fall back to the lowest register, a series of mixed black-and-white key downward arpeggios land us on the piano’s lowest Bb, which then returns us to the black-key pentatonicism of the opening.

The black/white division of notes in the mode disappears in the first half of the fugue, although scales in or jumps of sixths connects it to the prelude. The descending scale in sixths that starts at the end of the fugue subject continues once the next voice enters. It is here that the farce begins: the downward scale that lasts 4 beats in the first section extends to 6 beats in the second section, 8 to 10 in the third section, as many as 12 in the fifth section, and topping out at as many as 25 beats in the seventh section. What was once sublime (well, not bizarre, anyway!) becomes ridiculous.

The fourth and fifth sections of the piece are humorous in other ways, as well.  The third voice in the fourth section has trouble entering—almost like a rope jumper in Double Dutch trying to get in between the ropes, or like a less assertive person trying to enter into a conversation with a pompous blowhard: the harder the timid person tries the more the blowhard talks louder and longer…leading to the ridiculous overflowing of the scales in sixths.  This is the case even when the subject has been turned on its head, as it is in the fifth section, and in part in the seventh section as well.  It’s no accident, then, that the fifth section leads to a cascade of notes from the very top to the very bottom of the piano, while the seventh section features the most extended scale in sixths.

It’s because of this blowhard that I called this piece “The Pompous One” back in 2021. But even pompous people can be beautiful, in their way, and in the distillation of the outpouring of notes to the pentatonic black keys, ultimately ending at the last moment with a major chord, this piece succeeds. Along the way, there is a delightful mixture of pyrotechnics, humor, and charm and elegance. Mika does a fabulous job of bringing out all of the different mercurial moods of this monumental pair of pieces, as can be heard in this combined video.
